added_claim_errors: "(Part D is 63 days.)" and "Enroll in Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan within 63 days if your drug coverage isn't creditable": these mix up two rules. 63 days is the coverage gap that triggers the penalty. The enrollment window after employer coverage ends is 2 full months, and if the current drug coverage is not creditable, the penalty is already building.

Ties the no-penalty delay to the 400-employee size ("your coworker's penalty warning doesn't apply to you at 400 employees"). The SEP does not depend on employer size; the 20-employee line only decides who pays first. Minor imprecision.
"six-month Medigap open enrollment window (in most states)": the 6-month Medigap open enrollment is a federal right, so the 'most states' hedge is imprecise. Minor; state rules were not checked.

"That lets you delay Part B with no late-enrollment penalty" is attributed to the company being over the 20-employee threshold. The SEP does not depend on employer size; size only decides who pays first. Minor imprecision.

reasons: Both answers open by correcting the coworker's premise. Both say Part B can wait with no penalty under the 8-month SEP, flag COBRA, give a sound HR checklist, and include the HSA caveat on Part A. A covers more of the key. It gives the correct 2026 premium ($202.90/month, about $2,435 a year), says Part B would only be secondary coverage, notes that the Medigap open enrollment starts with Part B, and says Part D can wait with creditable coverage. B never gives the premium or mentions Medigap, and only touches on Part D through the creditable-coverage notice. B is tighter and has fewer side errors; A muddles the Part D timing by giving '63 days' as the enrollment window. Neither answer states the exception for a job or coverage that ends during the IEP. Both handle retirement steps only loosely, with no CMS-L564 and no CMS-40B. Taken together, A's fuller coverage outweighs B's concision by a small margin.
